messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 58

He is 35, a European man who has built a life around routine, patience, and predictability as a special education teacher. He lives alone and describes himself as someone who has always preferred a quiet, ordered world: the same coffee in the morning, the same route to work, the same careful planning around the demands of his classroom. Before the mugging, he moves through life with a steady, low-key confidence that comes from knowing how to anticipate other people’s needs, especially the children he teaches. He is not a man who seeks attention or conflict. He has learned to be observant, calm, and deliberate.

The assault happens on an ordinary evening, which is part of what makes it so difficult to absorb. He is walking home after buying groceries, carrying a bag in each hand, thinking about lesson plans for the next day. A man approaches too quickly, invading his space before he can decide whether to step aside. The exchange is brief and disorienting. He hears demands, sees the flash of threat in the other man’s posture, and feels the instant bodily shock of realizing he is being targeted. When he resists or hesitates, the mugger grabs him, shoves him, and takes what he has. He remembers the hard pavement, the smell of damp concrete, and the humiliating sense of being reduced to an object someone can push around. What stays with him most is not just fear, but the sudden knowledge that his body does not belong to him in that moment.

Afterward, he is shaken in a way he does not know how to explain. In the days that follow, he keeps replaying the event in fragments, as if his mind is trying to assemble a coherent version that might make it less absurd. He questions what he could have done differently: whether he should have handed over everything immediately, whether he should have shouted, run, or fought back. These thoughts circle with a punishing, almost forensic precision. At night, when he lies in bed, he replays the approach, the shove, the sound of his own breathing turning shallow. Sleep becomes lighter and more fragile. He wakes suddenly, already tense, with his heart racing before he is fully conscious of where he is.

His sense of safety begins to shrink. He avoids walking the same streets, especially after dark, and starts taking longer routes home even when it means arriving tired. He notices himself scanning doorways, parked cars, and passing faces with an intensity that feels exhausting. He is embarrassed by how much time he spends checking whether people are behind him. The city, once familiar, now feels full of unpredictable angles. He is jumpy when someone comes up too close, and he feels his muscles tighten before he has a chance to think. Loud voices or sudden movement make him flinch in a way he finds humiliating.

At work, he keeps functioning, but the effort is visible to him. In the classroom he is still gentle and patient, still able to recognize when a student is becoming overwhelmed, yet he finds himself more easily drained by noise, touch, and chaos. A child knocking over a chair or shouting unexpectedly can send a jolt through him that takes minutes to settle. He becomes more rigid about the room being orderly, the schedule being followed, the transitions being managed carefully. He does not want his students to see how strained he feels, so he works harder to appear composed. By the end of the day, he is depleted in a way that seems out of proportion to the work itself. He goes home and sits in silence, often not turning on music or television because even background sound feels like one more demand.

He also notices a change in how he feels about other people. He remains kind, but he is less open, less spontaneous. He turns down invitations more often. He does not like being caught off guard. He is aware that he is living in a narrower emotional range, as if part of him stays outside his own life watching for danger. There are moments when he feels detached from himself, as though the person who was shoved to the ground belongs to someone else. The mugging has not only frightened him; it has altered the way he moves through ordinary space, making every street, every stranger, and every unplanned encounter feel like a test he has to endure.
